# Parkinson-plus syndromes

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Neurocognitive disorders > Parkinson-plus syndromes*

[Original Article Link](/library/B30zkf)

---

## Summary

Parkinson-plus syndromes, also known as atypical parkinsonian syndromes, are a group of rare, adult-onset <u>neurodegenerative disorders</u> manifesting with <u>parkinsonism</u> and additional differentiating clinical features. Unlike in <u>Parkinson disease</u>, varying combinations of <u>basal ganglia</u>, cerebral cortical, <u>cerebellar</u>, <u>midbrain</u>, and/or <u>brainstem</u> structures are affected. <u>Differentiating features from Parkinson disease</u> (e.g., poor <u>levodopa</u> response, rapid progression, prominent early cognitive decline, and/or significant <u>autonomic dysfunction</u>) prompt consideration of a Parkinson-plus syndrome. Management is primarily symptomatic and supportive. The prognosis is less favorable than in <u>Parkinson disease</u>, with a more accelerated progression.

---

### Differentiating features from Parkinson disease




Features that distinguish Parkinson-plus syndromes from <u>Parkinson disease</u> include: [[1]](/library/bQaHu4)




* Motor features

* Early onset of <u>postural instability</u> with frequent falls

* Bulbar and speech disturbances (e.g., severe <u>dysarthria</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>)

* <u>Levodopa</u> responsiveness: poor or transient

* Pathological reflexes (e.g., <u>Babinski sign</u>)

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>: early involvement of the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>

* <u>Urinary incontinence</u>

* Cognitive impairment: early onset, progressive neurocognitive decline

* Disorder-specific symptoms, e.g.:

* <u>DLB</u>: <u>visual hallucinations</u>

* <u>PSP</u>: <u>vertical gaze palsy</u>

* <u>Corticobasal degeneration</u>: <u>alien limb phenomenon</u>

## Dementia with Lewy bodies

### Definition [[2]](/library/YGdnBr0)




<u>Dementia with Lewy bodies</u> (<u>DLB</u>) is an α-synucleinopathy characterized by the abnormal deposition of <u>Lewy bodies</u> (made of α-synuclein) in <u>neurons</u> primarily in cortical and subcortical <u>brain</u> regions.




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[3]](/library/Xsd9tr0)[[4]](/library/fsdk8r0)




* Second most common form of neurodegenerative <u>dementia</u>

* <u>Incidence</u>: 3–7% of all <u>dementia</u> diagnoses; increases with age [[3]](/library/Xsd9tr0)[[4]](/library/fsdk8r0)

* Mean age of onset: 75 years [[5]](/library/-udDF70)

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (up to 4:1) [[3]](/library/Xsd9tr0)





### Clinical features [[6]](/library/iHdJJr0)[[7]](/library/EHd8Hr0)




* Cognitive impairment: : early or concurrent <u>dementia</u> relative to motor symptoms  [[6]](/library/iHdJJr0)

* Motor features

* <u>Parkinsonism</u> (e.g., <u>bradykinesia</u>, <u>rest tremor</u>, rigidity) with poor response to <u>levodopa</u>

* <u>Postural instability</u> and frequent falls

* Neuropsychiatric features

* <u>Visual hallucinations</u> and <u>paranoid</u> episodes

* Fluctuations: episodic impairment of <u>cognition</u> and/or vigilance

* <u>REM sleep behavior disorder</u> (<u>RBD</u>) and <u>hypersomnia</u>

* <u>Mood disorders</u> (e.g., <u>depression</u>) and <u>anxiety</u>

* Increased <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>neuroleptic</u> medication

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Syncope</u>

* <u>Urinary incontinence</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Individuals with <u>dementia</u> with Lewy bodies have visual hallewynations.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Dementia</u> typically occurs within 1 year of motor symptom onset in <u>DLB</u> and is essential for diagnosis, whereas <u>dementia</u> typically develops later in <u>Parkinson disease</u> <u>dementia</u>. [[8]](/library/ZxdZEH0)




### Diagnosis [[6]](/library/iHdJJr0)[[9]](/library/OLXIBA)




#### General principles




* <u>DLB</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> supported by <u>neuroimaging</u>.

* Perform a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including <u>cognitive testing</u>.

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> excludes alternative diagnoses; findings may suggest <u>DLB</u>.

* Refer to <u>neurology</u> for <u>polysomnography</u>, <u>EEG</u>, and specialized investigations (e.g., <u>myocardial</u> <u>scintigraphy</u>).

* Definitive diagnosis requires postmortem neuropathological confirmation.





#### <u>Neuroimaging</u>




* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>: ↑ <u>Atrophy</u> of the <u>substantia innominata</u> and mesopontine <u>gray matter</u> and relative preservation of the <u>medial</u> <u>temporal lobes</u> compared to individuals with <u>Alzheimer disease</u>  [[10]](/library/JGdsZ70)

* <u>SPECT</u> or <u>PET-CT</u>: reduced <u>dopamine</u> transporter uptake in <u>basal ganglia</u>





### Pathology [[11]](/library/usdp9r0)




* Macroscopic

* <u>Cerebral atrophy</u>, particularly of the <u>frontal lobe</u>

* Relative sparing of the <u>hippocampi</u>

* Microscopic

* Lewy bodies; : α-synuclein positive, <u>hyaline</u> <u>cytoplasmic</u> <u>inclusions</u> (especially in cortical and subcortical <u>neurons</u>); cause neuronal degeneration

* <u>Lewy neurites</u>

* <u>Amyloid plaques</u>

* <u>Neurofibrillary tangles</u>





![Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites](media/yd2r3lzzuhkdzyzxjzjt0j8y.jpg)

Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites




### Treatment [[2]](/library/YGdnBr0)




#### General principles




* Symptom management is the primary goal.

* Management is led by <u>neurology</u> and supported by a multidisciplinary team (e.g., <u>psychiatry</u>, <u>physical therapy</u>).

* <u>Supportive care for dementia</u> and other nonpharmacological interventions (e.g., <u>behavioral therapy</u>) are indicated in all patients.

* Reserve pharmacological treatment for bothersome symptoms and limit <u>polypharmacy</u>.





#### Pharmacological treatment




* Cognitive impairment

* <u>Anti-dementia medications</u> (e.g., <u>AChEIs</u>, <u>memantine</u>)

* See “<u>Management of major neurocognitive disorders</u>.”

* Motor symptoms: <u>antiparkinson medication</u> (e.g., <u>levodopa</u>)   [[2]](/library/YGdnBr0)

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms

* <u>AChEIs</u>

* <u>Second-generation antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>quetiapine</u>, <u>clozapine</u>): Consider low dose for severe and/or refractory <u>psychotic features</u>.

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>:

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>: <u>medications for noncardiac syncope</u>

* <u>Bladder</u> symptoms: Consider <u>beta-3 agonists</u> (e.g., <u>mirabegron</u>) in consultation with urology.  [[12]](/library/B8dzK70)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Antipsychotic</u> treatment, especially with <u>typical antipsychotics</u>, is associated with severe <u>sensitivity</u> reactions, may worsen <u>parkinsonism</u>, and may precipitate a life-threatening <u>akinetic crisis</u>. [[2]](/library/YGdnBr0)




### Prognosis [[13]](/library/nGd7-r0)




* Variable prognosis; generally progresses more rapidly than <u>Alzheimer disease</u>

* Mean survival: 4–6 years from diagnosis  [[13]](/library/nGd7-r0)

* Common <u>causes of death</u> include <u>failure to thrive</u>, <u>pneumonia</u>, and complications from falls. [[14]](/library/twdXkH0)

## Multiple system atrophy

### Definition [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)




<u>Multiple system atrophy</u> (<u>MSA</u>) is an α-synucleinopathy characterized by the abnormal deposition of α-synuclein aggregates, primarily in <u>glial cells</u>, leading to neurodegeneration, including in the <u>substantia nigra</u>, <u>cerebellum</u>, <u>brainstem</u>, and <u>autonomic nervous system</u> structures.




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)




* <u>Incidence</u>: 1–3/100,000 individuals/year

* Mean age of onset: ∼ 56 years





### Clinical features [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)[[16]](/library/PsdWEr0)




* Motor features

* <u>Parkinsonism</u> (e.g., <u>bradykinesia</u>, <u>rest tremor</u>, rigidity) with poor response to <u>levodopa</u>

* <u>Postural instability</u>

* <u>Dystonia</u>

* Speech impairment (e.g., <u>dysarthria</u>, croaky voice due to <u>laryngeal dystonia</u>)

* <u>Dysphagia</u>

* <u>Stridor</u>

* Pyramidal signs (e.g., unexplained <u>extensor plantar reflex</u>)

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>

* Urinary symptoms (e.g., unexplained voiding difficulties)

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>

* <u>Cerebellar features</u>

* <u>Gait ataxia</u>

* <u>Limb ataxia</u>

* <u>Ataxic dysarthria</u>

* Oculomotor features (e.g., <u>nystagmus</u>)

* Neuropsychiatric features: <u>sleep disorders</u> (e.g., <u>RBD</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>MSA</u> is classified into two subtypes based on the predominant features at initial presentation: <u>MSA</u>-C (<u>cerebellar features</u>) or <u>MSA</u>-P (parkinsonian features).




### Diagnosis [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)




#### General principles




* <u>MSA</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> supported by <u>neuroimaging</u> findings.

* Perform a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including <u>cognitive testing</u>.

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> excludes alternative diagnoses; findings may suggest <u>MSA</u>.

* Definitive diagnosis requires postmortem neuropathological confirmation.





#### <u>Neuroimaging</u>




* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>

* Hot cross bun sign: a cross-shaped T2 <u>hyperintensity</u> on axial images of the <u>pons</u>  [[17]](/library/OvaIZ5)

* <u>Atrophy</u> of <u>putamen</u>, <u>middle cerebellar peduncle</u>, <u>pons</u>, and/or <u>cerebellum</u>

* <u>PET-CT scan</u>: hypometabolism in <u>putamen</u>, <u>brainstem</u>, or <u>cerebellum</u> [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)





![Hot cross bun sign](media/wmcgfh7jnx3bvmvo0dfv9nwu.jpg)

Hot cross bun sign




### Pathology [[18]](/library/aLXQwA)




* Macroscopic: olivopontocerebellar and striatonigral <u>atrophy</u>

* Microscopic: glial cytoplasmic inclusions

* Characterized by <u>gliosis</u> and axonal degeneration

* Glial and neuronal loss in the <u>substantia nigra</u>, <u>putamen</u>, <u>locus ceruleus</u>, <u>pontine nuclei</u>, <u>cerebellum</u>, and <u>inferior olivary nuclei</u>





### Treatment [[15]](/library/Ssdy8r0)




#### General principles




* Symptom management is the primary goal.

* Management is led by <u>neurology</u> and supported by a multidisciplinary team (e.g., urology, <u>occupational therapy</u>, <u>speech therapy</u>).

* Provide <u>nonpharmacological management of orthostatic hypotension</u> (e.g., <u>compression stockings</u>, ↑ salt intake).

* Reserve pharmacological treatment for bothersome symptoms.





#### Pharmacological treatment




* Motor symptoms

* <u>Parkinsonism</u>: <u>Antiparkinson medication</u> (e.g., <u>levodopa</u>) usually provides a poor or transient response.

* <u>Dystonia</u>: Consider <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections.

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>: <u>medications for noncardiac syncope</u> (e.g., <u>fludrocortisone</u>, <u>midodrine</u>, <u>droxidopa</u>)

* <u>Bladder</u> symptoms: Consider <u>beta-3 receptor</u> <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>mirabegron</u>) or <u>antimuscarinic agents</u> in consultation with urology.

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>: See “<u>Treatment of erectile dysfunction</u>.”

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms

* <u>Depression</u>: <u>antidepressants</u>

* <u>Sleep disorders</u>: Consider <u>melatonin</u> or <u>clonazepam</u>.





### Prognosis




Mean survival: 7–9 years  [[19]](/library/BnXzvA)

## Progressive supranuclear palsy

### Definition [[20]](/library/vsdA9r0)




<u>Progressive supranuclear palsy</u> (<u>PSP</u>) is a <u>tauopathy</u> characterized by the abnormal deposition of <u>tau protein</u> in the form of <u>neurofibrillary tangles</u>, causing <u>brain atrophy</u> and degeneration (e.g., in the <u>brainstem</u>, <u>basal ganglia</u>, and <u>frontal lobe</u>).




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[21]](/library/xnXEvA)




* <u>Incidence</u>: ∼ 1/100,000 individuals/year

* Mean age of onset: 60–70 years





### Clinical features [[7]](/library/EHd8Hr0)[[22]](/library/xHdEsr0)




* Motor features

* <u>Postural instability</u>

* Frequent unprovoked falls (often first symptom)

* Retropulsion

* <u>Parkinsonism</u> (e.g., gait <u>freezing</u>, <u>bradykinesia</u>, and axial rigidity)

* <u>Bulbar dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>dysarthria</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>, <u>dysphonia</u>)

* <u>Dystonia</u>

* Ocular features: : ranges from <u>vertical gaze palsy</u> (especially downward gaze) to complete external ophthalmoparesis

* Cognitive impairment: characterized by predominant <u>frontal lobe</u> abnormalities

* <u>Apathy</u>

* <u>Disinhibited behavior</u>

* Impaired reasoning

* Emotional lability (e.g., <u>pseudobulbar affect</u>)





### Diagnosis [[23]](/library/ZudZp70)




#### General principles




* <u>PSP</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> supported by <u>neuroimaging</u> findings.

* Perform a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including <u>cognitive testing</u>.

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> excludes alternative diagnoses; findings may suggest <u>PSP</u>.

* Definitive diagnosis requires postmortem neuropathological confirmation.





#### <u>Neuroimaging</u>




<u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> findings include the hummingbird sign, which represents <u>atrophy</u> of <u>midbrain</u> structures with a relatively intact <u>pons</u> region.  [[24]](/library/9HdNsr0)




![Hummingbird sign](media/x78ci3fy492q666v08bybxzc.jpg)

Hummingbird sign




### Pathology [[20]](/library/vsdA9r0)




* Macroscopic: <u>brain atrophy</u>

* <u>Frontal lobe</u>

* Pontomesencephalic area

* Lower <u>brainstem</u>

* <u>Nigrostriatal</u> pallidal area

* Microscopic: <u>neurofibrillary tangles</u>





### Treatment




#### General principles




* Symptom management is the primary goal.

* Management is led by <u>neurology</u> and supported by a multidisciplinary team (e.g., ophthalmology, <u>physical therapy</u>, <u>occupational therapy</u>).

* <u>Supportive care</u> and other nonpharmacological interventions (e.g., ophthalmological interventions for gaze palsy) are indicated in all patients.

* Reserve pharmacological treatment for bothersome symptoms and limit <u>polypharmacy</u>.





#### Pharmacological treatment [[23]](/library/ZudZp70)




* Motor symptoms

* <u>Parkinsonism</u>

* <u>Levodopa</u>: may provide a transient benefit [[23]](/library/ZudZp70)

* <u>Amantadine</u>: may reduce axial rigidity and improve mobility

* <u>Dystonia</u>: Consider <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections.

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms

* <u>Depression</u>: <u>SSRIs</u> (e.g., <u>citalopram</u> or <u>sertraline</u>)

* <u>Pseudobulbar affect</u>: <u>SSRIs</u> may improve symptoms.

* <u>Sleep disorders</u>: Consider <u>zolpidem</u>, <u>melatonin</u>, or short-term <u>benzodiazepines</u>.





### Prognosis




Median survival: ∼ 5 years  [[25]](/library/CHdqsr0)

## Corticobasal degeneration

### Definition [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)




<u>Corticobasal degeneration</u> is a <u>tauopathy</u> characterized by the abnormal deposition of <u>tau protein</u>, leading to degeneration primarily in the <u>cerebral cortex</u> and <u>basal ganglia</u>.




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)




* <u>Incidence</u>: ∼ 1/100,000 individuals/year

* Mean age of onset: ∼ 64 years





### Clinical features [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)[[27]](/library/oHd0rr0)




* Motor features: asymmetric, progressive motor abnormalities (e.g., <u>parkinsonism</u>, <u>dystonia</u>, and/or <u>myoclonus</u>) initially affecting only one limb

* Cortical features, e.g.:

* <u>Ideomotor apraxia</u>

* <u>Agnosia</u>

* Cortical sensory deficits

* Alien limb phenomenon; : involuntary yet purposeful movement of a limb, accompanied by the perception that it does not belong to the affected individual

* Cognitive impairment

* <u>Memory</u> deficit

* Language disturbances

* Neuropsychiatric features (e.g., <u>depression</u>)





### Diagnosis [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)




#### General principles




* <u>Corticobasal degeneration</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> supported by <u>neuroimaging</u> findings.

* Perform a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including <u>cognitive testing</u>.

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> excludes alternative diagnoses; findings may suggest <u>corticobasal degeneration</u>.

* Consider referral to <u>neurology</u> for specialized investigations (e.g., <u>SPECT</u> or <u>PET-CT scan</u>, <u>CSF</u> biomarkers).

* Definitive diagnosis requires postmortem neuropathological confirmation.





#### <u>Neuroimaging</u>




<u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> findings include asymmetric focal cortical <u>atrophy</u> and <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>basal ganglia</u>.




### Pathology [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)




* Macroscopic: asymmetric frontal and striatal <u>atrophy</u>

* Microscopic: intracellular <u>inclusions</u> of hyperphosphorylated <u>microtubule</u>-associated <u>tau protein</u> in neuronal and <u>glial cells</u>





### Treatment [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)




#### General principles




* Symptom management is the primary goal.

* Management is led by <u>neurology</u> and supported by a multidisciplinary team (e.g., <u>occupational therapy</u>, <u>speech therapy</u>).

* Nonpharmacological management is indicated in all patients (e.g., <u>physical therapy</u> may improve rigidity and prevent <u>contractures</u>).

* Reserve pharmacological treatment for bothersome symptoms and limit <u>polypharmacy</u>.





#### Pharmacological treatment




* Motor symptoms

* <u>Parkinsonism</u>: <u>Antiparkinson medication</u> (mainly <u>levodopa</u>) usually provides a poor or transient response.

* <u>Dystonia</u>: Consider <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections.

* <u>Myoclonus</u>: <u>clonazepam</u>

* Cognitive impairment: <u>AChEIs</u> (<u>off-label</u>) may be considered.

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms: Consider <u>antidepressants</u> for <u>depression</u>.





### Prognosis




Mean survival: ∼ 6.5 years  [[26]](/library/CnXqvA)
